summary: Codex runs its CI/CD entirely on GitHub Actions with 27 workflow files, most of them workflow_call reusables composed by two aggregate entry points: blocking-ci (every PR and push to main) fans into seven reusable gate workflows (Bazel tests on a 4-target matrix, cargo-deny, codespell, blob-size policy, repo checks, rust-ci fast checks, SDK checks) and a single always()-guarded 'required' fan-in job; postmerge-ci (push to main only) runs the heavier rust-ci-full cargo-nextest suite across five OS/arch platforms plus a V8 canary. Releases are tag-driven: pushing a rust-v*.*.* tag validates the tag against the Cargo.toml version, builds macOS/Linux-musl/Windows binaries, signs everything (rcodesign + Azure Key Vault notarization for macOS in a protected environment, cosign for Linux, Azure artifact signing for Windows), then creates a GitHub Release and fans out to npm (OIDC trusted publishing), a Cloudflare R2 mirror with mutable install.sh/channel aliases, DotSlash manifests, WinGet, and a Vercel deploy hook for developers.openai.com. Separate tag families release the Python SDK/runtime to PyPI, a patched zsh, and rusty-v8 builds. Hygiene is unusually strong - all ~195 external action references are SHA-pinned and checkouts set persist-credentials: false - but the release path itself runs no test suite on the tagged commit, relying on the tag pointing at CI-validated main history.

findings.title: Two aggregate CI entry points, four release tag families, two schedules
findings.description: The trigger surface is deliberately narrow: blocking-ci runs on every pull request and on pushes to main and is the single merge-blocking entry point; postmerge-ci runs only on pushes to main for the heavier suites. Releases are driven by four tag families - rust-v*.*.* (main CLI release), codex-zsh-v*.*.* (patched zsh helper), python-v* (Python SDK to PyPI), rusty-v8-v*.*.* (V8 builds). Two scheduled workflows exist (rust-release-prepare every 4 hours, close-stale-contributor-prs daily), three issue-triage workflows react to issue events, and cla.yml uses pull_request_target. Roughly half of the 27 workflow files are workflow_call reusables invoked by the two entry points, which keeps the required-check list in one version-controlled place.

evidence.note: PR trigger of the single merge-blocking entry point
post-merge entry point runs on pushes to main only

findings.title: Every 4 hours a bot refreshes models.json and opens a reviewed PR
findings.description: rust-release-prepare runs on a 0 */4 * * * schedule (and manual dispatch), curls the ChatGPT backend models endpoint with a secret API key, rewrites codex-rs/models-manager/models.json, and opens an automated pull request via peter-evans/create-pull-request with two named reviewers. The change therefore still passes through the normal PR gate rather than being pushed to main directly - a sane pattern for keeping generated data fresh. The job is restricted to the openai/codex repository and runs in a dedicated 'rust-release-prepare' environment.

evidence.note: fetches model metadata from the backend
changes land as a PR, not a direct push

findings.title: Issue triage is automated with Codex itself
findings.description: Three issue-event workflows (issue-deduplicator, issue-labeler, issue-translator) run Codex via the openai/codex-action to deduplicate, label, and translate newly opened issues - the project dogfoods its own agent inside its pipeline. The jobs are gated to the canonical openai/codex repository so forks do not burn Actions minutes or need secrets.

evidence.note: Codex runs as a CI step

findings.title: Release builds: macOS x2 archs x2 bundles, static musl Linux x2 archs, Windows via sub-workflow
findings.description: On a rust-v tag, the build job matrix produces per-target bundles: aarch64/x86_64-apple-darwin each in a 'primary' bundle (codex, codex-code-mode-host, codex-responses-api-proxy, plus a DMG) and an 'app-server' bundle, and x86_64/aarch64 Linux builds that intentionally ship MUSL-linked static binaries (bundling bwrap) built on self-hosted xl runners. Windows x64/arm64 binaries come from the reusable rust-release-windows workflow. Builds use CARGO_NET_GIT_FETCH_WITH_CLI, packed split debuginfo on macOS (dSYMs archived, then binaries stripped), and cargo-chef cache pre-warming elsewhere in CI; the job has a 90-minute timeout to absorb long release builds.

evidence.snippet: # Release artifacts intentionally ship MUSL-linked Linux binaries.
evidence.note: static Linux linking is a deliberate distribution choice

findings.title: Workspace version is 0.0.0 on main; release commits must stamp the real version
findings.description: codex-rs/Cargo.toml carries workspace version 0.0.0 in regular history, yet the release workflow's tag-check job fails unless the pushed rust-v tag exactly matches the version in Cargo.toml. Together these imply that release tags are not cut on ordinary main commits: some step outside the repo's visible automation (a release branch, manual commit, or external tooling) writes the real version into Cargo.toml and tags that commit. No workflow or script in the repo performs this version bump, so the version-stamping half of the release process lives outside what is checked in here.

evidence.note: tag must equal Cargo.toml version, so a release commit must set it

findings.title: PRs get Bazel tests + fast checks; the full cargo-nextest 5-platform matrix runs post-merge
findings.description: The merge-blocking suite runs `bazel test //...` on a 4-target matrix (macOS arm64/x64, Linux gnu/musl; arm Linux disabled as flaky) plus fast cargo-native checks (fmt, clippy, cargo-shear, benchmark smoke test). The full cargo-nextest test suite - macOS aarch64, Linux x64 (remote-env) and arm64, Windows x64 and arm64, largely on self-hosted runners with sccache - runs only after merge via postmerge-ci calling rust-ci-full, with an opt-in '**full-ci**' branch-name trigger for developers who want the full suite pre-merge. This trades PR latency for a window where platform-specific cargo test regressions are only caught post-merge; the Bazel PR matrix and the opt-in escape hatch are the compensating controls.

findings.title: Hand-rolled path-based change detection scopes the fast PR jobs
findings.description: rust-ci's first job diffs the PR against its base with plain git (explicitly avoiding an external action) and emits booleans (codex, argument_comment_lint, workflows) that gate the downstream jobs, so a docs-only PR skips Rust jobs. Any change under .github/ flips the 'workflows' flag and forces the full fast bundle - a safe default that prevents CI edits from skipping their own validation. Manual dispatches force everything on.

evidence.snippet: - name: Detect changed paths (no external action)
evidence.note: deliberate avoidance of third-party path-filter actions
CI changes force the full run

findings.title: Single always()-guarded required job closes the skipped-check loophole
findings.description: Instead of listing many required checks in branch protection, blocking-ci funnels all seven gate workflows into one 'CI required' job that runs with always() and executes check_ci_results.py, which fails unless every dependency reports an explicit 'success' - skipped and cancelled count as failures. This closes the classic GitHub Actions hole where a skipped required check appears green, and keeps the required-check list version-controlled in one file. postmerge-ci reuses the same script so the two entry points cannot drift in result interpretation.

evidence.note: fan-in job runs even when dependencies fail

findings.title: Merge gates beyond tests: cargo-deny, codespell, blob-size, unused-deps, clean-worktree checks
findings.description: The PR gate includes cargo-deny (license/advisory/ban checking over the Rust workspace), codespell, a blob-size policy check, repo-checks, cargo-shear with --deny-warnings (unused dependency detection), a custom argument-comment dylint lint, and a CLA gate. Distinctively, nearly every job ends with a 'Check for a clean worktree' step, which fails if any build or codegen step modified tracked files - a repo-wide codegen-freshness gate that keeps generated artifacts (lockfiles, protobuf output, etc.) in sync with their sources.

evidence.snippet: - name: Check for a clean worktree

findings.title: CLA gate uses pull_request_target with write permissions - but never checks out PR code
findings.description: cla.yml runs contributor-assistant on pull_request_target and issue_comment events with contents/pull-requests/statuses write permissions, storing signatures on a cla-signatures branch. pull_request_target with write tokens is the classic CI privilege-escalation trigger, but this workflow never checks out or executes PR code - it only runs the pinned contributor-assistant action - so the risky trigger is used correctly. Worth preserving: any future edit that adds a checkout of the PR head to this workflow would create a serious vulnerability.

evidence.note: write token in the privileged context
only step; no PR code checkout

findings.title: rust-v tag: validate, build, sign, GitHub Release, then fan out to npm/R2/DotSlash/WinGet
findings.description: Pushing an annotated rust-v*.*.* tag runs the whole release: tag-check enforces the tag format (x.y.z with optional -alpha/-beta suffixes) and that it equals the Cargo.toml version; after building and signing, the release job assembles all artifacts plus SHA256SUMS manifests and installer scripts, generates release notes from the tagged commit's message, and creates the GitHub Release (prerelease/latest flags derived from the version suffix). Downstream jobs then publish DotSlash manifests, mirror everything to Cloudflare R2 in two stages (assets, then channel finalize), publish six platform npm packages plus the @openai/codex wrapper and SDK to npm via OIDC trusted publishing (stable and numbered-alpha versions only), open a WinGet PR for stable versions, trigger a Vercel deploy of developers.openai.com, and force-update the latest-alpha-cli branch pointer once R2 and npm have succeeded.

evidence.snippet: # Publish to npm using OIDC authentication.

findings.title: Every platform's binaries are signed: AKV-notarized macOS, cosign Linux, Azure-signed Windows
findings.description: The release pipeline signs artifacts on all three platforms: macOS binaries and DMGs are signed with rcodesign against Azure Key Vault via PKCS11 and notarized with Apple, inside a protected 'codesigning' GitHub environment, with signature-info reports archived for verification; bundled helper binaries (rg, patched zsh) are fetched, signed, and notarized too. Linux artifacts are signed with sigstore cosign via a local composite action; Windows binaries go through an 'azure-artifact-signing' environment. Checksum manifests (codex-package_SHA256SUMS) accompany the release, and the R2 mirror re-verifies digests before advancing channel aliases. This is a notably complete signing story for a CLI distributed through curl-installers and package managers.

evidence.note: macOS signing gated by a protected environment

findings.title: The release path runs no tests - a tag on any commit builds, signs, and publishes
findings.description: rust-release's publish job depends only on tag-check, the build jobs, macOS finalization, and lint asset packaging - no test suite executes anywhere in the release workflow. The integrity model relies on tags being cut from CI-validated main history, but nothing in the pipeline enforces that: anyone with permission to push a rust-v tag on an arbitrary commit (including one never reviewed or tested) triggers a fully signed release to GitHub, npm, R2, and WinGet. Protected environments (codesigning, codex-r2-publisher) can add reviewer gates for signing and mirroring, but the GitHub Release and npm publish steps are not visibly environment-gated in the workflow. A tag-provenance check (verifying the tagged commit is contained in main) or a smoke-test job before publish would close the gap.

evidence.note: release job dependencies contain no test job
any matching tag push starts the release

findings.recommendation: Add a job to rust-release that verifies the tagged commit is an ancestor of main (git merge-base --is-ancestor) and/or run a smoke-test suite on the built artifacts before the publish jobs; alternatively gate the GitHub Release/npm jobs behind a protected environment with required reviewers, and restrict rust-v* tag creation via a tag ruleset.

findings.title: Users receive Codex via npm, curl-installers backed by R2, GitHub Releases, WinGet, PyPI, DotSlash
findings.description: Distribution is artifact-based with many channels: @openai/codex and platform packages on npm; install.sh/install.ps1 bootstrap scripts served from Cloudflare R2 (publish_r2_release.py uploads every release under a versioned prefix with digest verification, then advances mutable codex/channels/latest and codex/install.sh aliases for stable releases); GitHub Releases with SHA256SUMS; WinGet (OpenAI.Codex) via an automated winget-pkgs PR; the Python SDK on PyPI pinning an openai-codex-cli-bin runtime wheel; and DotSlash manifests. The install.sh script verifies the sha256 digest of every downloaded archive against release metadata and falls back from R2 to GitHub Releases on failure, so the payload (though not the bootstrap itself) is integrity-checked end to end.

evidence.snippet: Stable releases also update the mutable ``codex/install.sh`` and
evidence.note: mutable install channel aliases on R2

findings.title: No workflow deploys a running service - backend deployment lives elsewhere
findings.description: Every pipeline in the repo ends at artifact publication; nothing deploys or promotes a server environment. The only deployment-shaped step is a best-effort curl to a Vercel deploy hook that refreshes developers.openai.com's config schema after stable releases, marked continue-on-error at both job and step level so it can never fail a release. The Codex cloud backend the CLI talks to (chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex, referenced by the models-refresh job) is evidently deployed from a separate private codebase.

evidence.note: deploy hook is best-effort, cannot fail the release

findings.title: All ~195 external action references are SHA-pinned; checkouts drop credentials
findings.description: Every third-party action reference across all 27 workflows (195 of 195 external `uses:` lines) is pinned to a full 40-character commit SHA with a human-readable version comment, and composite actions under .github/actions follow the same rule. Checkout steps consistently set persist-credentials: false so later steps cannot reuse the git token. Combined with mostly-explicit least-privilege permissions blocks and repository guards on scheduled/issue jobs, this is top-tier GitHub Actions supply-chain hygiene; the criticism findings elsewhere in this report should be read against that baseline.

evidence.note: representative SHA-pinned action with version comment

findings.title: The curl-able install bootstrap is a mutable, unsigned R2 object
findings.description: publish_r2_release.py deliberately maintains mutable aliases - codex/install.sh, codex/install.ps1, and codex/channels/latest - that stable releases overwrite in place. Users who bootstrap via the R2-hosted installer execute whatever shell script currently sits behind that alias; unlike the release archives (which the script verifies by sha256 against release metadata), the bootstrap itself has no signature or pinned digest, so R2 write credentials (the codex-r2-publisher environment secrets) are sufficient to silently change what new installs run. This is inherent to every curl-pipe-sh channel and the blast radius is limited to the installer, but it makes the R2 credentials and their environment protection the single most security-sensitive secret in the pipeline.

evidence.snippet: ``codex/install.ps1`` bootstrap aliases from their verified versioned assets.
evidence.note: mutable bootstrap aliases documented in the publisher
R2 credentials scoped to a dedicated environment

findings.recommendation: Require reviewers on the codex-r2-publisher environment if not already enforced, and consider publishing a detached signature or checksum for install.sh at a well-known URL (or serving the installer from GitHub Releases only) so security-conscious users can verify the bootstrap before piping it to a shell.
